## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\alpha,\beta>0$, the nonnegative function
$p\mapsto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ and
$$\int_{(0,1)}p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\,d\lambda_1(p) =B(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)} \in(0,\infty).$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice and positive real numbers $\alpha,\beta$.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom assumed by the bounded-Riemann-to-Lebesgue integral theorem. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The real Beta function is the improper integral of $p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ on $(0,1)$. [[def-real-beta-integral]].

[F2] For positive $\alpha,\beta$, $B(\alpha,\beta)=\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)$. [[thm-real-beta-gamma-identity]].

[F3] The Euler Gamma integral is finite and strictly positive for every positive argument. [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

[F4] A bounded Riemann-integrable function on a closed bounded interval is Lebesgue measurable and has the same Lebesgue and Riemann integrals under Countable Choice. [[thm-bounded-riemann-integrable-functions-are-lebesgue-measurable-and-have-the-same-integral]].

[F5] Continuous functions on a closed bounded interval are bounded and Riemann integrable. [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]].

[F6] Increasing limits of nonnegative measurable functions have integrals equal to the increasing limit of their integrals. [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]].

[F7] The improper Beta integral converges for positive parameters. [[thm-real-beta-integral-convergence]].

[F8] Positive real powers are continuous on $(0,\infty)$. [[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]].

[F9] The integral is with respect to the stated Lebesgue measure. [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice and $\alpha,\beta>0$.

1.1 By [F8], $f(p)=p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is continuous and hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ with the measure in [F9]. For each integer $m\ge2$, its restriction to $[1/m,1-1/m]$ is continuous, hence bounded and Riemann integrable by [F5], and [F4] identifies its Lebesgue integral with its Riemann integral. The indicators of these intervals increase pointwise to one, so the truncated functions increase to $f$. [A1, F4, F5, F8, F9, construct]

2.1 By [F6], the Lebesgue integral of $f$ is the limit of the truncated integrals from step 1.1. The same truncations define the improper integral in [F1], which converges by [F7]; therefore the limit is $B(\alpha,\beta)$. [step 1.1, F1, F6, F7]

3.1 The identity in [F2] and positivity and finiteness in [F3] show that $B(\alpha,\beta)$ is finite and strictly positive. This proves the displayed Lebesgue integral identity and its endpoint bounds. [step 2.1, F2, F3] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $p,q>0$, define $B(p,q)=\int_0^1t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt$.

The integral is improper at both endpoints. The exact convergence theorem [[thm-real-beta-integral-convergence]] proves that it exists precisely for the displayed positive parameters and therefore discharges the definition's existence obligation.
For $p,q>0$, $B(p,q)=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q)$.
Let $s$ be real. The Euler integral $\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ converges if and only if $s>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $p,q$ be real. The Beta integral converges if and only if $p>0$ and $q>0$.

Here the Beta integral means $\int_0^1t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$,
$$\int_{\Delta_{k-1}}\prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j-1}\,dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1} =\frac{\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}\in(0,\infty).$$
Consequently the density kernel in [[def-dirichlet-density-kernel]] has
integral one.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, $k\ge2$, and $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k>0$.

[A1] Countable Choice is required for the stated nonnegative Lebesgue change-of-variables theorem. [[def-countable-choice]].

[F1] The simplex and its nonnegative density kernel are defined in coordinate Lebesgue measure by [[def-dirichlet-density-kernel]].

[F2] A $C^1$ diffeomorphism between open sets changes variables in a nonnegative Lebesgue integral under Countable Choice. [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F3] Tonelli factors a nonnegative product integral over a finite sigma-finite product space into iterated integrals. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F4] For $u,v>0$, the one-dimensional Beta integrand has Lebesgue integral $B(u,v)=\Gamma(u)\Gamma(v)/\Gamma(u+v)$, finite and positive. [[lem-beta-density-normalization]].

[F5] The Beta-Gamma identity holds for positive arguments. [[thm-real-beta-gamma-identity]].

[F6] Gamma values at positive arguments are finite and positive. [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]].

## Proof

**Given:** Countable Choice, $k\ge2$, and positive $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k$.

1.1 Define the stick-breaking map from $(0,1)^{k-1}$ to $\Delta_{k-1}$ by $p_i=z_i\prod_{j<i}(1-z_j)$ for $i<k$. Its inverse is $z_i=p_i/(1-\sum_{j<i}p_j)$, so it is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism. Its derivative matrix is lower triangular with diagonal entries $\prod_{j<i}(1-z_j)$; hence its Jacobian is $\prod_{i=1}^{k-2}(1-z_i)^{k-i-1}$. [A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Under this change of variables, each factor $p_j^{\alpha_j-1}$ contributes $z_j^{\alpha_j-1}$ and a factor $(1-z_i)^{\alpha_j-1}$ for each $i<j$; the Jacobian adds exponent $k-i-1$ to $1-z_i$. Thus the transformed integrand is $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}z_i^{\alpha_i-1} (1-z_i)^{\sum_{j>i}\alpha_j-1}.$ This factorization is valid because all coordinates and residuals are strictly positive on the open cube. [step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Tonelli [F3] and [F4] now give the integral as $\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}B\!\left(\alpha_i,\sum_{j>i}\alpha_j\right).$ Applying [F5] to each factor cancels the intermediate Gamma terms and leaves $\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)/\Gamma(\alpha_+)$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F6] the displayed ratio is finite and positive. Multiplying the integrand by the reciprocal constant in [F1] therefore gives integral one, which proves normalization. [F1, F6, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $k\ge2$ and positive coordinates $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k$, write
$\Delta_{k-1}=\{(p_1,\ldots,p_{k-1})\in(0,\infty)^{k-1}:
\sum_{j<k}p_j<1\}$ and set $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. The **Dirichlet density
kernel** is the nonnegative function
$$q_\alpha(p_1,\ldots,p_{k-1}) =\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_{j=1}^k\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_{j=1}^kp_j^{\alpha_j-1},\qquad \alpha_+=\sum_{j=1}^k\alpha_j,$$
relative to coordinate Lebesgue measure $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$. This item
defines the density function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For every $\alpha,\beta>0$, the nonnegative function
$p\mapsto p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}$ is Lebesgue measurable on $(0,1)$ and
$$\int_{(0,1)}p^{\alpha-1}(1-p)^{\beta-1}\,d\lambda_1(p) =B(\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)}{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)} \in(0,\infty).$$
For $p,q>0$, $B(p,q)=\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)/\Gamma(p+q)$.
Let $s$ be real. The Euler integral $\int_0^\infty t^{s-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ converges if and only if $s>0$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g(A) \subseteq B$, and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$. If $g$ is continuous
at $c$ and $f$ is continuous at $g(c) \in B$, then $f \circ g$ is continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $g$ is continuous on $A$ and $f$ is continuous on $B$, then
$f \circ g$ is continuous on $A$.

**No side hypothesis is needed, and that is the whole point.** The composition
theorem for limits, [[thm-composition-of-function-limits]], must assume one of
two extra conditions: either $L \in B$ with $f(L) = M$, or $g \ne L$ on a
punctured neighbourhood of $c$; with both dropped the statement is false, which
is [[fs-naive-composition-of-limits]]. The first of those conditions is exactly
*continuity of $f$ at $L$* written out, so under the hypotheses above it holds
automatically and nothing has to be assumed. The mechanism is visible in the
proof: [[def-continuity-real]] quantifies over $|y - b| < \rho$ rather than over
$0 < |y - b| < \rho$, so the value $y = b$ that the limit version cannot control
is precisely the one the continuity hypothesis does control.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a
sigma-finite measure, and let $(P_\eta)_{\eta\in\Omega}$ be a nonempty
exponential family of [[def-exponential-family]] with density
$p_\eta(y)=h(y)\exp\{\eta^TT(y)-A(\eta)\}$. For each finite $n\ge1$, the IID
sample law $P_\eta^{\otimes n}$ has density
$$\prod_{i=1}^nh(y_i)\exp\!\left\{\eta^T\sum_{i=1}^nT(y_i)-nA(\eta)\right\}$$
relative to $\mu^{\otimes n}$, and
$T_n(y_1,\ldots,y_n)=\sum_{i=1}^nT(y_i)$ is sufficient for the sample.
No full-rank, completeness, or converse characterization is asserted.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the standard-Borel sample space, sigma-finite $\mu$, and a
nonempty family with the displayed exponential-family density.

[A1] The Axiom of Choice is assumed by the common-reference factorization criterion and its conditional-law suppliers. [[def-axiom-of-choice]].

[F1] An exponential-family density is $p_\eta=h\exp\{\eta^TT-A(\eta)\}$ and integrates to one against $\mu$. [[def-exponential-family]].

[F2] Finite product sigma-algebras are generated by measurable rectangles, and finite products of sigma-finite measures are sigma-finite and satisfy the rectangle formula. [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]] [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

[F3] Tonelli integrates nonnegative product densities by iterated integrals. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]].

[F4] A nonnegative measurable density induces a measure by integration. [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

[F5] Measures agreeing on a generating pi-system with a finite exhaustion agree on the product sigma-algebra. [[thm-measure-uniqueness-on-a-sigma-finite-pi-system]].

[F6] The finite sample product of standard-Borel spaces is standard Borel, and the finite-dimensional Euclidean statistic space $\mathbb R^k$ with its Borel sigma-algebra is standard Borel. [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]] [[lem-finite-euclidean-space-is-standard-borel]].

[F7] If every likelihood ratio relative to one in-model reference law is a Borel function of a statistic, the statistic is sufficient on standard-Borel spaces. [[thm-common-reference-factorization-criterion]].

[F8] Sufficiency means there is one conditional-law kernel of the data given the statistic that works for every parameter. [[def-sufficient-statistic]].

[F9] Measurable functions are closed under finite products and sums. [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]].

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 For fixed $\eta$, each coordinate pullback of $p_\eta$ is measurable on the product sigma-algebra [F2], and the product density $g_\eta(y_{1:n})=\prod_i p_\eta(y_i)$ is measurable by [F9]. Its integral against $\mu^{\otimes n}$ is one by [F2], repeated Tonelli [F3], and $\int p_\eta\,d\mu=1$. Thus $g_\eta\,d\mu^{\otimes n}$ is a probability measure by [F4]. On every measurable rectangle it equals $\prod_iP_\eta(A_i)$ by the rectangle formula and Tonelli, so the sigma-finite pi-system uniqueness theorem [F5] identifies it with the IID product law. Expanding $g_\eta$ gives the density displayed in the Statement. [F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F9, given]

2.1 Since $\Omega$ is nonempty, choose $\eta_0\in\Omega$. The density ratio on the common support is $\frac{g_\eta(y_{1:n})}{g_{\eta_0}(y_{1:n})} =\exp\{(\eta-\eta_0)^TT_n(y_{1:n})-n(A(\eta)-A(\eta_0))\}.$ If any $h(y_i)=0$, both product densities vanish, so the same positive Borel function of $T_n$ satisfies $g_\eta=r_\eta(T_n)g_{\eta_0}$ everywhere. Integrating this identity on each measurable set proves that it is a version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative under $P_{\eta_0}^{\otimes n}$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, choose]

3.1 By [F6] both the sample and the finite-dimensional statistic spaces are standard Borel. The reference $P_{\eta_0}^{\otimes n}$ belongs to the family, and step 2.1 makes every likelihood ratio a Borel function of $T_n$. Applying [F7] gives a common conditional-law kernel, which is sufficiency by [F8]. The sole choice-axiom use is inherited from [A1] and [F7]. [A1, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, given] ∎

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be standard Borel, let $\mu$ be a $\sigma$-finite positive measure, let $h:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$ be a measurable statistic. For $\eta\in\mathbb R^k$ put

$$Z(\eta)=\int h(x)e^{\eta\cdot T(x)}\,\mu(dx),\qquad H=\{\eta:0<Z(\eta)<\infty\},\qquad A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta).$$

For a parameter set $\Omega\subseteq H$, the associated **exponential family** has laws $P_\eta$ with density

$$p_\eta(x)=h(x)\exp\{\eta\cdot T(x)-A(\eta)\}\quad(\eta\in\Omega).$$

The normalization $A(\eta)=\log Z(\eta)$ makes each density integrate to one. In this item **full-rank** means that $\Omega$ contains a nonempty open subset of $\mathbb R^k$ and there do not exist $b\ne0$ and $c\in\mathbb R$ with $b\cdot T=c$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{h>0\}$. A parameter set containing an open subset is also called regular in some sources; terminology varies, so this definition controls here. The condition is stronger than needed for the completeness theorem below but rules out redundant displayed coordinates.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be standard Borel, let $\Theta\ne\varnothing$, and let $T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y$ be a statistic. Fix $\theta_0\in\Theta$ and set $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$. Assume $P_\theta\ll P_0$ for every $\theta$. Then $T$ is sufficient if and only if for every $\theta$ the Radon–Nikodym derivative $dP_\theta/dP_0$ has a $\sigma(T)$-measurable version. Equivalently, for each $\theta$ there is a Borel $g_\theta:\mathcal Y\to[0,\infty)$ with $dP_\theta/dP_0=g_\theta(T)$ $P_0$-almost surely. The null exceptional set may depend on $\theta$. The requirement $P_0\in\{P_\theta\}$ is essential; an arbitrary external dominating probability is not covered.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Under AC, standard Borelness gives each law an individual conditional law through [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]] and [[lem-regular-conditional-kernels-factor-through-a-standard-borel-conditioning-variable]]; sufficiency additionally asks that one kernel works across parameters.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
